trig-vectors-scalars-and-vectors.title: Scalars and vectors
trig-vectors-scalars-and-vectors.summary: Recognize magnitude-only scalar quantities and directed vectors, read vector notation, and compute displacement from initial and terminal coordinates.

blocks.text: A scalar describes magnitude with appropriate units (such as mass or speed). A vector describes both magnitude and direction (such as displacement, force, or velocity). In Cartesian coordinates, a directed segment from A to B is the component vector B−A; equal vectors have the same components regardless of where they are drawn.

blocks.caption: Cartesian vector components and vector notation: resolve directed displacement along horizontal and vertical axes.

blocks.title: Displacement from A(−2,4) to B(3,−1)
blocks.strategy: Subtract terminal minus initial coordinates, component by component.
blocks.check: The net displacement points right and downward regardless of the path traveled.

blocks.title: Compare the vectors from (1,2) to (4,6) and from (−2,1) to (1,5)
blocks.problem: Compare the vectors from (1,2) to (4,6) and from (−2,1) to (1,5)
blocks.strategy: Use component differences to test equality, not the locations of their tails.
steps: Second vector is (1−(−2),5−1)=(3,4), so they are equal.
blocks.check: Translation does not change a free vector.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Distance and displacement are not interchangeable: distance is a nonnegative scalar, while displacement has direction. Do not subtract initial from terminal in the wrong order.

blocks.answer: Velocity is a vector; speed is a scalar.
blocks.explanation: Velocity includes direction, whereas speed records only the magnitude of motion.

blocks.text: Reference guide (original wording and independently designed examples): Sullivan, Trigonometry: A Unit Circle Approach, 9th ed., §§5.4–5.7; Lial et al., Trigonometry, 10th ed., §§7.4–7.5; Kelley, The Humongous Book of Trigonometry Problems, Chs. 14–16. For cross products and 3D orientation, see Sullivan §§5.6–5.7; Young, Trigonometry, 3rd ed., Ch. 7. Applied force and work examples use standard vector conventions and should be reviewed with engineering-mechanics references.

trig-vectors-magnitude-and-direction.title: Magnitude and direction
trig-vectors-magnitude-and-direction.summary: Find vector length and orientation using Pythagorean geometry and quadrant-aware angles; use the appropriate reference direction.

blocks.text: The length of a vector is its Euclidean magnitude. The direction angle in the xy-plane is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis unless otherwise stated. atan2(y,x) returns the correct signed quadrant; a positive angle in [0°,360°) can be obtained by adding 360° when necessary.

blocks.caption: Vector length and direction angle measured from the positive horizontal axis; signs locate the correct quadrant.

blocks.title: Find magnitude and standard angle of v=(−3,4)
blocks.problem: Find magnitude and standard angle of v=(−3,4)
blocks.strategy: Calculate the length, then resolve the angle in quadrant II.
steps: The reference angle is arctan(4/3)≈53.13°. As x<0 and y>0, θ≈180°−53.13°=126.87°.
blocks.check: atan2(4,−3) gives the same quadrant-II direction.

blocks.problem: Recover the vector with magnitude 10 at 30°

blocks.text: Ordinary arctan(y/x) alone cannot identify the correct quadrant. Direction of the zero vector is undefined. Specify whether angles use degrees or radians.

blocks.explanation: Compute √(8²+15²)=√289=17; the direction is in quadrant IV.

trig-vectors-rectangular-vector-componen.title: Rectangular vector components
trig-vectors-rectangular-vector-componen.summary: Resolve a given magnitude and direction into signed x/y components; reconstruct resultant vectors and extend component notation into three dimensions.

blocks.text: Any plane vector can be expressed as the sum of its x- and y-directed projections. A positive counterclockwise mathematical direction differs from compass bearings measured clockwise from north. Three-dimensional component vectors use an additional z-coordinate.

blocks.caption: A vector resolved into orthogonal horizontal and vertical components, with orientation measured from +x.

blocks.title: Resolve a 20 N force at 150° from +x
blocks.problem: Resolve a 20 N force at 150° from +x
blocks.strategy: Use the exact unit-circle sine and cosine signs.
steps: F_y=20sin150°=10 N; force points left and upward.

blocks.title: Reconstruct a vector with components (3,−4)
blocks.strategy: Compute the hypotenuse and quadrant-aware direction.
steps: Direction is atan2(−4,3)≈−53.13° or 306.87° measured counterclockwise.
blocks.check: The negative y-component agrees with quadrant IV.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: An angle measured from north is not automatically interchangeable with one measured counterclockwise from east. Keep physical units on components and distinguish 2D from 3D magnitude.

blocks.prompt: What are the components of 8 units at 270°?
blocks.explanation: cos270°=0 and sin270°=−1, so the vector lies on negative y.

trig-vectors-vector-addition-and-subtrac.title: Vector addition and subtraction
trig-vectors-vector-addition-and-subtrac.summary: Combine or subtract vectors componentwise to calculate displacement, force and velocity resultants, including differences that represent relative motion.

blocks.text: Add or subtract corresponding components. The geometric head-to-tail rule agrees with component arithmetic. Relative velocity of object A with respect to object B is v_A−v_B; this is a vector difference, not the difference of magnitudes.

blocks.caption: Vector components allow resultants to be calculated algebraically, even when arrows point in different directions.

blocks.title: Find the resultant of (3,4) and (−1,2)
blocks.check: Head-to-tail addition ends at (2,6) when starting at the origin.

blocks.title: Find velocity of A relative to B for v_A=(12,2), v_B=(4,−3)
blocks.problem: Find velocity of A relative to B for v_A=(12,2), v_B=(4,−3)
blocks.strategy: Subtract the reference velocity to express motion in B’s frame.
steps: Therefore relative velocity is (8,5), in the same units as the input.
blocks.check: Adding v_B back to relative velocity recovers v_A.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not add magnitudes unless the vectors are parallel and aligned. Subtraction depends on operand order; v_A−v_B is the negative of v_B−v_A.

trig-vectors-unit-vectors-and-normalizat.title: Unit vectors and normalization
trig-vectors-unit-vectors-and-normalizat.summary: Construct direction-only vectors by dividing by magnitude, identify the zero-vector exception, and convert between magnitudes and unit directions.

blocks.text: A unit vector has magnitude exactly one. For a nonzero vector v, the normalized vector v/||v|| points in the same direction. The standard basis vectors i, j and k each have length one. The zero vector cannot be normalized.

blocks.caption: A normalized vector preserves an arrow’s direction but changes its magnitude to exactly one.

blocks.title: Normalize v=(3,4)
blocks.strategy: Calculate the length before dividing components.

blocks.title: Find a unit vector in direction (−2,1,2)
blocks.problem: Find a unit vector in direction (−2,1,2)
blocks.strategy: Apply the same normalization rule in three dimensions.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Never divide by the length of the zero vector. A vector with components between −1 and 1 is not necessarily a unit vector; check its total magnitude.

blocks.answer: Its magnitude is zero, so normalization divides by zero.
blocks.explanation: The direction of the zero vector is not determined.

trig-vectors-dot-product-and-angle-betwe.title: Dot product and angle between vectors
trig-vectors-dot-product-and-angle-betwe.summary: Use the scalar dot product to test perpendicularity, recover the angle between nonzero vectors, compute projections, and calculate work.

blocks.text: The dot product multiplies corresponding components and sums them. It equals the product of the vector magnitudes and cosine of their included angle. For nonzero vectors, a zero dot product means orthogonality; a zero vector makes angle determination undefined.

blocks.latex: \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf b}\mathbf a=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{\|\mathbf b\|^2}\mathbf b\quad(\mathbf b\ne\mathbf0)

blocks.caption: Two vectors form an included angle; the dot product measures their directional alignment.

blocks.title: Are a=(2,1) and b=(1,−2) perpendicular?
steps: Both vectors have nonzero length, so cosθ=0 and θ=90°.
blocks.check: Their component slopes are negative reciprocals.

blocks.title: Find the angle between (1,0) and (1,√3)
blocks.strategy: Use the dot product and lengths.
steps: Dot product is 1 and the magnitudes are 1 and 2.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: The result of a dot product is a scalar, not a vector. The angle formula requires both vectors to be nonzero; the projection formula requires a nonzero base vector.

blocks.prompt: What is the dot product of (2,3) and (4,−1)?

trig-vectors-cross-product-and-orientati.title: Cross product and orientation
trig-vectors-cross-product-and-orientati.summary: Compute three-dimensional cross products with correct signs, apply the right-hand rule, and interpret the magnitude as an area or moment arm.

blocks.text: The cross product of two 3D vectors is perpendicular to both, with direction fixed by the right-hand rule. Its magnitude is ||a||||b||sinθ. Swapping the order reverses its direction. For 2D vectors embedded in the xy-plane, the z-component equals a_x b_y−a_y b_x.

blocks.caption: In a right-handed coordinate system, +x crossed with +y points along +z; reversing operands reverses orientation.

blocks.title: Compute i×j
blocks.strategy: Apply the cyclic right-handed basis convention.

blocks.title: Compute (1,2,0)×(3,0,0)
blocks.strategy: Evaluate all three Cartesian cross-product components.
blocks.check: The result points along negative z, as required by the right-hand rule for the chosen operand order.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Cross products are not commutative: a×b=−(b×a). Do not confuse the scalar dot product with the vector cross product. A planar 2D cross-product shorthand represents only the signed z-component.

blocks.prompt: What is j×i in a right-handed basis?

trig-vectors-applications-in-2d-and-3d.title: Applications in 2D and 3D
trig-vectors-applications-in-2d-and-3d.summary: Model resulting forces, relative velocities, work, torque, and navigation in two and three dimensions, checking units and sign conventions.

blocks.text: Engineering quantities are commonly combined as vectors. Force or velocity resultants use componentwise addition. Mechanical work uses the dot product between force and displacement; torque about an origin uses the cross product from position to applied force. Choose a coordinate system and sign convention before calculating.

blocks.caption: Force, displacement and position require different vector operations: dot for work and cross for torque.

blocks.title: Drone ground velocity: 4 m/s east and wind 3 m/s north
blocks.problem: Drone ground velocity: 4 m/s east and wind 3 m/s north
blocks.strategy: Add the velocity vectors along independent axes.
steps: Speed is √(16+9)=5 m/s, at atan2(3,4)≈36.87° north of east.
blocks.check: The east and north components reproduce the stated wind and air motion.

blocks.title: Torque from a 5 N upward force 2 m to the right of origin
blocks.problem: Torque from a 5 N upward force 2 m to the right of origin
blocks.strategy: Use position crossed with force, not force crossed with position.
steps: Position vector r=(2,0,0) m; force F=(0,5,0) N.
blocks.check: Right-hand rotation from +x to +y points toward +z.

sections.title: Common mistakes, checkpoint, and reference guide

blocks.text: Do not add speeds as scalars when directions differ; do not compute work with a cross product or torque with a dot product. Confirm units (J for work, N·m for torque) and reference-axis conventions.
